title: Two notes, one missing word

beats.say: Cover the two endings. A diver writes, “The tide rises near the ...” A robin’s field note is open beside it. This little model gives reef and tree an even chance on either page. Which word would you put in the diver’s note?

The diver wrote reef. A park note uses tree, where a robin builds its nest. This model has one dial for both notes. Suppose training on the diver’s sentence turns it toward reef. What happens to the chance of tree in the park note?

Turn the dial. A training step raises the score for reef by a quarter and leaves the score for tree at zero. We call those scores logits. Reef now gets about fifty-six percent on either note. Look at the park page. Tree has fallen from half to just under forty-four percent.

A real language model can use context to tell the notes apart. When we take a pretrained model and keep training it to predict the next token in licensed field notes, that is continued pretraining. We will trace an update, mix in other text, then choose a checkpoint to test on real work.

title: What would fix the incident reply?

beats.say: At three in the morning an incident assistant tells the on-call engineer to check the Wi-Fi. Which two steps should it recommend? The runbook says the worker pool runs out of connections when the gateway retries. The retry needs jitter, and token reissue needs an idempotency token.
What could we change before spending a single training step?

Put the excerpt in the prompt and leave the weights alone. Suppose the answer now follows the runbook. That gives us a retrieval baseline. If it still fails, compare direct supervised tuning with domain pretraining followed by supervised tuning. What would you hold fixed to isolate the extra stage?

Use the same supervised recipe on both paths. Hold the runbook excerpt, prompt, decoding, held-out incidents and scoring fixed. Then compare the two assistants. Supervised examples can teach facts and procedures as well as answer format.

Supplying evidence takes context. Triple the prompt length and this square of full-attention pairs grows ninefold at fixed model width. Other work, including projections, feed-forward layers, retrieval and cache reuse, affects the actual latency. Time the supported answer and score its accuracy. Even a name that takes several tokens can make sense in context.

title: Choose an experiment for each observation

beats.say: The assistant says the limit is eight retries. The current release note says four. Which experiment could correct that answer today? Retrieve the current note and ask again with the same weights. Now look at the held-out logs. On eighteen of twenty lines, the model gives the actual next token less than a one percent chance. Try continued pretraining on separate runbooks, then score the same held-out lines again.

Here the incident reply gives the right code but leaves out the required action. Test supervised fine-tuning with complete example replies, and count missing fields on fresh incidents. Now compare two valid replies. Both call for jitter and token reuse. Reviewers prefer the one that leads with the retry instruction. Test preference training using pairs ranked on that criterion.

Each experiment uses a different signal. The release note supplies a fact at answer time. Runbooks supply next tokens, demonstrations supply complete replies, and reviewers supply a ranking. Check whether the change helps the assistant on held-out incidents.

title: Which prompt rows receive a gradient?

beats.say: Follow the two shaded prompt rows into the sum. They make the hidden vector that the fixed output head uses to predict the response. The head gives the third class the lowest score. That class is our observed response.
We score only that response and skip the earlier prompt target. Which input rows will its loss reach?

Trace the response gradient back through the sum. Both shaded rows feed the prediction, so both receive a gradient. The loss is about one point eight six two nats. The third row was never looked up. Its input gradient is zero here.
If we tied the input and output weights, there would be another path through the head.

The mask tells us which predictions to score. The sum tells us which inputs influenced that score. A separate choice tells the optimizer which parameters it may change. This small model uses a sum and a fixed head so we can check those paths directly.

title: How many targets count?

beats.say: Take a block of seven tokens. With no earlier context, the first token gives us something to read. From there we can score the next six. In general, a block of n tokens scores n minus one positions before padding or boundary masks.
Add up the negative log probabilities on the positions you actually score, and divide by their count. You need at least one.

Exponentiate that mean loss and you get perplexity. Compare the same target positions with the same available context. All six are eligible in our continued-pretraining example. A response-only mask leaves four direct targets. The other tokens can still supply context to those predictions.

Runbook text teaches the model which pieces follow each other in a runbook. Supervised replies teach it what to say to the engineer. Their serializer and mask specify which reply positions count. Either objective can update the full model or just an adapter, depending on which parameters you leave trainable.

title: How many pieces does the timeout code use?

beats.say: Try the payment service’s timeout code in this small longest-match tokenizer. It knows lowercase timeout as one piece. In the uppercase identifier it recognizes AUTH. The underscore and each remaining letter fall back to a single character. That makes nine pieces in this vocabulary. A production tokenizer has its own vocabulary and splitting rules.

Those nine pieces spend more context than one. Measure corpus-wide token lengths with the actual checkpoint tokenizer before assigning a multiplier to all documents. If a whole sequence triples in length, its full-attention pair component grows ninefold at fixed width. Total forward work and measured latency include other operations.

Keeping the existing vocabulary preserves its ID coordinates and matrix shapes. Continued pretraining does not automatically merge the nine pieces into a new token. Subwords can still represent the concept, so evaluate held-out text fit and incident tasks. High fertility is an inspection signal rather than proof that a vocabulary extension will improve quality.

title: What changes when we add a token?

beats.say: Switch to a second toy tokenizer with the five entries shown here. Give it a different spelling, all lowercase, with no underscore. Starting at the left, which IDs will it emit for this word? Choose the longest entry that fits, write down its ID, and continue from the first unused letter. It reads auth, then time, then out. Their IDs are zero, one and two.

Suppose we want this spelling to have one ID. The input table needs a row to read it and the output head needs a row to predict it. Add the new row to both tables and register the whole spelling as ID five in the tokenizer. The old IDs stay in place. Update the configuration too. For K new tokens each table gains K rows of the same width. Preserve shared weights when the tables are tied. Here the two tables are separate.

Look up the three IDs the old tokenizer emitted. Each input row has eight numbers. In each column, average the values in rows zero, one and two. Those eight means initialize input row five for the whole word.
The output head still needs its own treatment, and a held-out task must tell us what the model learned.

In a Hindi vocabulary study, researchers tried several ways to initialize Nemotron’s new rows. Would you choose the same method after a short training run? Look at the starting losses. Of these two methods, weighting subwords by character count in both tables gives the lower loss. After fifty training steps, the order flips. The researchers used held-out loss at that point to choose an initializer. Their choice gives each input subword equal weight and rescales the new input vector to the median length of the existing Hindi vectors. For the output row, it weights each subword by character count. The researchers tested that method against the Mean-all baseline on Hindi questions. At five hundred steps, the selected method scored about fifty-seven percent correct and the baseline scored thirty-two percent.

title: What happens to an old word’s probability?

beats.say: Use a separate two-word output head so we can count every term. Keep its two rows and the hidden vector fixed. Both dot products are zero. Each old word contributes one unit to the softmax denominator, so the words split the probability evenly. The proposed new row is their mean. Its dot product is also zero.
When we add it, what probability will the first word get?

The denominator gains a third unit mass while the old logits remain zero. The old target probability becomes one third. Its negative log probability rises from about zero point six nine three to one point zero nine nine, an increase of natural log three halves, about zero point four zero five.

The new output row reduced an old word’s probability even though its logit stayed fixed. Starting with three unit masses, suppose we give a fourth word the same score. What probability would an old target get, and how much would its loss rise?

Add the fourth unit mass. Each old probability falls from one third to one quarter. Subtract the old loss, log three, from the new loss, log four. The increase is the natural log of four thirds. Training and downstream retention still need measurement.
Code Llama mostly retained the Llama tokenizer and added four special infilling markers; that is one documented design, not a general threshold for extending every domain vocabulary.

title: Prepare domain text before training

beats.say: Start with the documents the model should learn from. Remove boilerplate, corrupted extraction, near-duplicates, and text that the team has no right to use. Keep licensing, provenance, language, and date metadata beside each source so stale material can be removed later.
Split evaluation material before training and check for overlap with source documents. Deduplication reduces repeated passages, while careful lineage keeps the held-out measurement meaningful.

Tokenize with the checkpoint's tokenizer, inspect how important terms break into pieces, and record the tokenizer version. A vocabulary extension changes embeddings and makes perplexity comparisons more delicate.

title: Which revisions must stay together?

beats.say: Two revisions of a runbook can have different file names and almost the same text. Give them one group name before splitting. Hash each group name with SHA two fifty-six and take the remainder after division by four. Bucket zero goes to validation.
The other buckets go to training. Every revision carrying that name travels together.

On these inputs the auth and S D K groups go to training. Payments and webhooks go to validation. No group name appears in both. But give two copies different names and this check can pass even when their text leaks across the split. Someone has to identify the revision families first.

Hash bucketing targets a fraction across many groups, not exactly one quarter of tokens in a small corpus. Check sizes, topic coverage and residual overlap. A common source, revision family or deduplication group can carry leakage across otherwise distinct filenames. Grouping and content screening protect different evidence paths.

title: Which sources can enter training?

beats.say: Read the source manifest. Each row records training rights, privacy scrubbing and whether the source is reserved for evaluation. The last column before the decision gives the token count. Which sources can enter training, and how many tokens would you admit in total?

Only the public A P I docs clear all three checks. Their count is an integer, so eight hundred thousand tokens can enter training. The on-call notes still need scrubbing. The probes are reserved for evaluation. The vendor export lacks training rights.

The flags record review decisions someone already made. This function checks their types and values. Put quotation marks around true and you get a string, so the flag is invalid. A token count must be a nonnegative integer. The boolean true also fails that check. License verification and privacy review happen upstream.

Preserve access restrictions and a removal path alongside provenance, language, date and source revision. A sensitive domain source may need stronger controls than public text. Quality, rights, privacy and evaluation isolation are separate decisions on the same document owner, before its tokens enter the training stream.

title: Would this screen catch a copied runbook?

beats.say: For this screen, lowercase each text and collapse its whitespace. Hash the result for comparison. The timeout candidate matches a held-out runbook even though its case and spaces changed. Drop that candidate. Use normalization to compare documents. Preserve the original spelling and spacing of any text you retain for training.

If case distinguishes two service names, normalization can merge different identifiers. Code indentation can carry meaning too. Conversely, a partial copy or paraphrase can escape a whole-document hash. Choose a comparison policy for the source, group near-duplicates and audit what remains.

Go back to the field notes. D one survived and will supply the sentence about the tide. D six matches a held-out example, so it stays out of training. That decision belongs with the source record all the way through tokenization.

title: Where does the last document go?

beats.say: Switch to a separate packing example. These four documents, P one through P four, all passed screening. Their rows contain token IDs. Read left to right, then continue on the next row. Append a zero to mark each document end. That gives fourteen positions. The packer returns full blocks of six. Will the last document fit into a full block on this call?

Fill the first six slots. They take all of P one, including its end marker, and the first two tokens of P two. Fill the next six slots. That block starts with the end marker from P two and holds all of P three. Which pair is still waiting?
Carry the last two tokens forward. Token forty-one and its end marker both belong to P four. They start the next packing call together.

If every shard drops its tail, short or rare sources can disappear. Back in block one, the usual shift gives five targets. Token twenty-one starts P two, yet causal attention can still reach back into P one across the end marker. To isolate the documents, restrict attention to tokens from the same document and mask the target pairs that cross a boundary.

title: What does the field note teach?

beats.say: Back in the field collection, D one is the note we kept. It ends in reef. Our checkpoint tokenizer splits that word into two pieces. The model has read up to the word “the.” Look at the two pieces below. Which one is the next target?

First it predicts the piece spelled R E. Score the probability it gave that piece, then add the observed piece to the context. Now it predicts E F. The period gets its own turn. Each scored position contributes the negative log probability of the piece that actually came next.

Return to the two-word model from the opening. Reset the dial to even odds so we can replay the same update. Reef is one outcome and tree is the other. Each observed word costs about point six nine three nats. If we raise the reef score, which note will cost more?

Turn the reef score up by a quarter. The same probability moves in both notes. Read the loss under each one. The diver’s observed reef now costs point five seven six nats. The park observer’s tree costs point eight two six. A shift that helped one sentence made the other more surprising.
A single parameter has to serve them both. On a real checkpoint, test that trade on unseen text and on the work people need it to do.

title: What happens to the first update?

beats.say: A released checkpoint might give us just the weights. Restoring a full training run also restores optimizer moments and the scheduler position. Record which state you start from. A tiny learning rate can leave the domain poorly fitted. A large step may damage general performance. The loss curve alone cannot tell you which circuit changed.

With ordinary gradient descent, multiply the gradient by the learning rate and reverse its sign. Adam W also keeps two moving averages, one for the gradient and one for its square. Start them at zero.
After the first gradient, bias correction gives back the gradient and its square. Here those are minus a half and a quarter.

Divide the corrected gradient by the square root of its corrected square, plus epsilon. Ignoring weight decay, this first coordinate moves up by almost one learning rate. Ordinary gradient descent would move it up by half a learning rate. Zero-initialized moments alone don’t make the step explode.
Later updates depend on the history and precision. That makes warmup a choice to test on the new data.

title: Choose a learning rate for the new starting point

beats.say: The base model has already made many updates, so resuming at a tiny final learning rate may adapt too slowly. Teams often test a short warm-up followed by a decay from a selected peak. Warm-up lets optimizer state settle before the largest updates are applied.
The curve here is one authored schedule. Compare peak rates and warm-up lengths while keeping the data and evaluation protocol controlled.
Larger steps can improve domain fit and also move the model farther from its broad starting behavior. The best checkpoint comes from measured task outcomes and declared regression limits.

title: What rate applies at step nine?

beats.say: The last curve used display units. Our worked example runs for a thousand updates. Its five percent warmup takes the first fifty. The scale is in millionths, with a floor of three and a peak of thirty. During warmup we add a fraction of the distance from floor to peak.
Step zero takes the first fiftieth. At step nine, what fraction have we used, and what rate does that give?

Step nine takes ten fiftieths of the rise. A fifth of twenty-seven is five point four. Add the floor of three and the rate is eight point four millionths. Step zero used three point five four millionths. By step forty-nine all fifty warmup increments are in, so we reach thirty millionths.

Pull back to the full run. Step fifty starts the cosine decay at the same peak. Follow the curve down to the floor. Its progress runs from zero to one over nine hundred forty-nine step intervals. That puts the final update, step nine hundred ninety-nine, at three millionths.

Ibrahim and colleagues varied warmup duration from zero to two percent and saw similar validation losses after fifty billion tokens in those runs. In a separate sweep they held warmup at one percent and tried half, equal and double the original peak rate, and the higher peaks improved prediction on the new text and increased loss on the old text.
Use matched data to sweep rates for your checkpoint, then compare downstream gain and general regression.

title: Which unlabeled text should the model read?

beats.say: Domain-adaptive pretraining uses unlabeled material from the domain, such as the incident runbooks and API corpus. Task-adaptive pretraining uses the task’s own unlabeled inputs, possibly a much smaller subset. The original Don’t Stop Pretraining experiments used masked-language-model RoBERTa across domains and classification tasks.

Those names describe the text we select. The original masked-model study gives us a reason to try the experiment. To measure what transfers to this causal model, compare raw continuations first. Then compare both complete assistants after the same supervised tuning. Few response labels and abundant relevant text make this comparison worth running.

Recall the reply that quoted eight retries when the release note said four. Test retrieval of the current note. For the missing action field, test supervised demonstrations and check the template. When reviewers rank two valid replies, test a preference method on ranked examples. Compare held-out performance and cost for the failures your assistant actually shows.

title: Mix in examples from the original distribution

beats.say: Replay adds a fraction of general text to the new domain stream. Its purpose is to keep selected broad examples contributing to the same next-token objective. A token-counted replay share can differ from a document-counted share when examples have different lengths.

Restore this same shared logit to zero before each controlled mixture comparison. In a one-parameter teaching model, domain examples push the logit upward and replay examples push it downward. At a quarter replay, the weighted gradient changes from minus point five to minus point two five.

That arithmetic explains the mixture; a useful replay percentage depends on the model and the measured capabilities to preserve. The fraction of scored tokens matters, and separate domain-only and replay-only controls help interpret results.

title: What does replay replace?

beats.say: Fix the window at two million processed tokens. Start with five percent replay. That gives us one hundred thousand replay tokens and one million nine hundred thousand domain tokens. If we raise replay to a quarter, how many domain tokens will it displace?
Now half a million tokens are replay and the other one and a half million are domain text. Replay displaced four hundred thousand domain tokens. We kept the total number of processed tokens constant.

In this sampler, F labels a field block and R labels a replay block. Choose fifteen field blocks and five replay blocks. Shuffle that window with a fixed seed. Five out of twenty is also one quarter of the scored targets if every block scores the same number. A real loader must advance its cursors in both sources before taking the next window.

Python rounds ties to even: one quarter of ten blocks is two point five, so this window function chooses two replay blocks, realizing twenty percent. Log the actual target share. A fractional accumulator or probabilistic source sampler can approach the requested share over time.
Equal token budgets are a compute proxy only under comparable model, lengths, masks and execution.

Bloomberg G P T trained from scratch, rather than continuing a released base checkpoint. Its roughly seven-hundred-nine-billion-token assembled inventory was about fifty-one percent financial and forty-nine percent public text; it consumed five-hundred-sixty-nine billion tokens. Inventory shares are not the exact mixture consumed by training. That historical mixture cannot prescribe replay for this domain shift.

title: How much replay reaches the update?

beats.say: Return to the twenty-block sampler window. Five come from replay. Each block starts with six targets after the usual shift. Now mask four targets in every replay block. Each colored cell still counts and each dash is skipped. If you pool the losses from all the colored cells, what fraction comes from replay?
Give every colored cell equal weight. The fifteen field blocks contain ninety targets. The five replay blocks have just ten between them. That gives replay one tenth of the weight in the pooled mean.
At logit zero the field gradient is minus a half and replay’s is plus a half. Ninety votes one way and ten the other give a mean gradient of minus point four.

Suppose we meant replay to have a quarter of the weight. Take the mean within each source, then give replay a quarter and the field notes three quarters. Each target still belongs to the same block. Their influence changes, and the gradient returns to minus a quarter.

Giving every block equal weight happens to agree here because blocks within each source have equal target counts. You can also change sampling to deliver the target mix. Check what the trainer averages after masks, including when it accumulates microbatches.

title: Does better text prediction help the assistant?

beats.say: Use a held-out set of domain documents. As training proceeds, the domain perplexity falls from forty-two to twenty-six. The model is getting better at predicting that text. At the start, the assistant got sixty-two percent of the incident tasks right. From the new text score alone, can we tell whether it now solves more incidents?

Score the incidents at each checkpoint. The task stays at sixty-two percent all the way across. Text prediction improved, but we have yet to see a task gain here. If the domain text still fits poorly, we may be underfitting it. Check corpus quality, training steps and learning rate before increasing the budget.

Now score general text on those same checkpoints. Its perplexity rises. To find out whether an ability has slipped, test it directly. Set the limits before the run. In this example the last checkpoint solves seven of ten safety cases and six of ten reasoning cases.
Both miss their stated minimums. Losing a previously demonstrated ability as the model adapts is called forgetting.

These perplexity curves used a fixed tokenizer, context, scoring boundaries and target masks. What if one candidate changes the tokenizer? We still want to compare how well both models predict the same text.

title: Which tokenizer fits these thirty bytes better?

beats.say: Both reports score the same thirty bytes with the same context, boundaries and target text. The coarse tokenizer uses ten tokens. The fine tokenizer splits them more finely and uses twenty. To get token perplexity, divide each total loss by its own token count, then exponentiate. Which row has the smaller average loss per token?

Fine wins per token. Eighteen nats over twenty tokens gives a smaller mean than fifteen over ten. Now change the divisor to bytes. Both rows have exactly thirty. Dividing the total loss by thirty gives nats per byte.
Divide again by the natural log of two to get bits per byte. Which tokenizer now costs less?

Coarse costs less per byte. It spends about point seven two bits per byte on this text. Fine spends about point eight seven. The finer split had more tokens to spread its loss across, while the number of scored bytes stayed fixed.
To choose an actual vocabulary, also test domain tasks and retained abilities after adaptation.

title: How do two documents contribute to perplexity?

beats.say: Keep the tokenizer and scoring rules fixed. The first document has sixty nats of loss over twenty targets. The second has one hundred sixty over forty. Give each target the same vote by adding the losses and adding the counts.
The pooled mean is two hundred twenty divided by sixty. Exponentiate once to get a corpus perplexity of about thirty-nine point one.

Suppose we first computed a perplexity for each document and then averaged the two. We’d get about thirty-seven point three. That gives the short document equal weight and averages after exponentiating. Apply the pooled rule separately to domain and general text. In the example on the right, domain perplexity falls while general perplexity rises.

A domain-loss decrease measures text fit. It does not identify memorization, prove reasoning gain or impose a logical prerequisite on downstream improvement. Entity-span losses need explicit subword alignment and weighting. Compare base plus S F T with continued pretraining plus the same S F T when that is the intended final product.

title: Which required abilities survive training?

beats.say: Follow the same ten safety cases and ten reasoning cases across these checkpoints. The team requires nine correct on safety and seven on reasoning. At the start, the model gets all ten safety cases and eight reasoning cases right. By the end, it gets seven and six.
The last checkpoint misses both requirements in this example.

General text perplexity is a separate signal from those tasks. Freeze the evaluation texts, tokenizer, masks, available context, prompt format and scoring protocol. Historical benchmarks can supply anchors, but inspect contamination, ceilings and the private tasks required by this product. Safety must be checked by its actual specified suite.

An accuracy move from seventy percent to sixty-eight percent is two percentage points. The relative reduction is two divided by seventy, about two point eight six percent. Declare the unit when setting a regression budget. Otherwise two thresholds that look numerically similar can select different checkpoints.

title: Choosing a checkpoint under a retention budget

beats.say: Use a different example run for checkpoint selection. Its base general perplexity is nineteen point two. Before looking at candidates we allow a rise of at most one and a half points. Put the ceiling at twenty point seven. A reading right on the line passes.

Here are the three training checkpoints. Each dot shows general perplexity on the same scale. Beside it you can read task accuracy and domain perplexity for that very checkpoint. Which checkpoint exceeds our ceiling?

Twelve thousand steps is too far. It has the lowest domain perplexity in the table, but its general perplexity rose by four point seven. Set that row aside. If we want the best task accuracy among the remaining rows, which one do we keep?

Keep the four-thousand-step checkpoint. Seventy-two percent beats both earlier task scores, and its general perplexity rose by only point nine. We would consult domain perplexity to break a tie. These scores chose the checkpoint, so we need fresh cases to check it.

Open the reserved set for that one checkpoint. In this example it gets fourteen of twenty cases right. On the reserved general text its perplexity rises by point nine against the base model on that same text.
Save the weights, tokenizer and configuration, corpus manifest and hash, and token counts. Keep the evaluation protocol with the scores. Save optimizer state as well if you plan to resume this run.

title: Has another training step earned its cost?

beats.say: Plot those same four checkpoints. Moving right means the model fits domain text better. Moving up means it fits general text worse. The horizontal line is our budget. The dot farthest right belongs to the twelve-thousand-step checkpoint. It buys its extra domain gain at a price the team already ruled out.

Moving along these four dots always improves one measure at the expense of the other. They form a Pareto frontier. To dominate a dot, another would need to do at least as well on both axes and strictly better on one.

Our task-first ranking supplies a decision the frontier alone cannot make. Before ranking, the picker checks for finite perplexities of at least one and task accuracy from zero to one hundred percent, including both endpoints.

Choosing among saved checkpoints is one decision. Deciding to spend another hour training is another. Suppose one more answer turns correct on the same five hundred cases. That moves accuracy by two tenths of a percentage point. Is it worth another hour?
Apply the minimum worthwhile gain, patience window and regression limits set before the run. Allow for uncertainty and evaluation cost, then confirm the selected recipe on reserved cases.

title: Which weights are allowed to change?

beats.say: LoRA can train on domain next-token text or on supervised prompt-response data. QLoRA additionally stores a frozen quantized base and propagates derivatives into trainable low-rank adapters. Those are parameter and storage choices, while continued pretraining and S F T identify supervision and data choices.

Frozen base embeddings stay fixed even when their representations influence a scored prediction. Follow a single path with input two. The frozen base weight is three, so that branch contributes six. Let A equal one. If an update moves B from zero to a half, the adapter contributes one. Their sum moves from six to seven. The base branch still contributes six.

Choose the objective from the observed failure, then choose full-weight or parameter-efficient training under the budget and deployment constraints. Code Llama Instruct combined code pretraining with instruction tuning.
Llama three’s code expert used continued pretraining, S F T and D P O before helping produce annotations and synthetic data. These are examples, not compulsory stages for every domain.

Save the selected weights with their tokenizer, configuration, corpus manifest and evaluation protocol. To resume exactly, also keep optimizer and scheduler state, random-number state and both loader cursors. Otherwise the next window can repeat tokens or skip them.
The small moment vectors in the field-note example illustrate what the record holds. Promotion still depends on reserved outcomes from the actual assistant.

title: A fresh run for the on-call assistant

beats.say: Try a smaller training window. Four field blocks each score three targets. Two replay blocks each score one. We start at logit zero again, with gradients of minus a half for field targets and plus a half for replay. Pool the targets. What share belongs to replay, and what mean gradient reaches the logit?

Count the two replay targets among all fourteen. Replay gets one seventh. Twelve negative halves and two positive halves sum to minus five. Divide by fourteen for the mean gradient. Suppose we average the six block means equally instead. What happens when each replay target gets a whole block’s vote?
Replay jumps to a third, and the gradient shrinks to minus one sixth. Restore equal weight per target to recover the pooled update.

That calculation tells us how we trained. To choose a checkpoint, we need measurements. For this new run the base general perplexity is eighteen and the allowed rise is one. Here are three candidates.
Apply the ceiling, compare task accuracy, and break a tie with lower domain perplexity. Which candidate would you take to the reserved incidents?

B crosses the ceiling. Its eighty-two percent is tempting, but nineteen point two exceeds the limit of nineteen. A and C both score seventy-eight percent on the task. Which of those two has the lower domain perplexity?
Choose C. Its domain perplexity is twenty-one against A’s twenty-two. We only needed that column because the eligible task scores tied.

Back to the on-call team. Give both assistants the same reserved incident and the same runbook excerpt. One assistant starts from the base model. The other starts from C. Both get the same supervised tuning. Hide the model names while scoring. The runbook calls for jittered retries and reuse of the idempotency token.

Try the rubric on these two example replies. One says to wait exactly one second and reuse the token. The other says to randomize the retry delay and reuse the token. Which reply satisfies both requirements?

Both replies reuse the token. Only the second one adds jitter. It meets both requirements, while the first misses the timing requirement. Score both assistants this way across the reserved incidents. Their difference tests what extra pretraining bought us. Check the required general abilities again before deploying.
